title: Sustainable Development Goal 14

definition.text: The UN goal 'Life below water': to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources.

facts.text: It has ten targets, covering marine pollution, ecosystem protection, ocean acidification, sustainable fishing and conserving coastal and marine areas.
Target 14.5 aimed to conserve at least 10 per cent of coastal and marine areas by 2020, measured by protected-area coverage.
Target 14.4 is measured by the share of fish stocks within biologically sustainable levels.
Ocean pH now averages 8.1, about 30% more acidic than in pre-industrial times.
Sustainable fisheries made up roughly 0.1 per cent of global GDP in 2017.
Oceans cover over 70% of Earth's surface, yet from 2013 to 2021 only 1.1% of national research budgets went to ocean science.
The World Economic Forum estimates US$175 billion a year of blue finance is needed to achieve SDG 14.

related: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

title: Harmful fisheries subsidies
article: Sustainable Development Goal 14#Target 14.6: End subsidies contributing to overfishing

definition.text: Government payments to fishing fleets that encourage overcapacity, overfishing or illegal fishing, which SDG Target 14.6 aims to end.

facts.text: Capacity-enhancing subsidies help developing countries compete with large fishing nations, but bring no long-term benefit if they cause overfishing.
The WWF estimates illegal fishing costs up to $36.4 billion a year globally.
The Global Biodiversity Framework likewise asks countries to stop subsidising destructive activities such as industrial fishing.

title: Large-scale marine protected areas
article: Sustainable Development Goal 14#Large-Scale Marine Protected Areas (LSMPAs)

definition.text: Marine protected areas of at least 100,000 square km, set up to cut overfishing and human disturbance of ocean ecosystems.

facts.text: Concerns about them span resource management, conflicts between rival countries, and trade-offs between people's needs and the environment.
The management challenge is inadequate monitoring and enforcement of protection measures.

title: Sustainable Development Goal 15

definition.text: The UN goal 'Life on land': to protect, restore and sustainably use land ecosystems, manage forests, combat desertification and halt biodiversity loss.

facts.text: It has 12 targets to be achieved by 2030, measured by 14 indicators.
Outcome targets include ending deforestation, restoring degraded land, protecting habitats and sharing benefits from genetic resources fairly.
Forests cover roughly 4 billion hectares, or 30.7 per cent of the world's land; 93 percent are natural and 7 percent planted.
Target 15.5 on threatened species is measured by the Red List Index.
Target 15.9 asks countries to build ecosystem and biodiversity values into national planning and accounts.
As of 2023 there was about a $700 billion gap in financial support for low-income countries to protect biodiversity.
Deforestation is estimated to have risen by 12% from 2019 to 2020.

related: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

title: Land degradation neutrality
article: Sustainable Development Goal 15#Target 15.3: End desertification and restore degraded land

definition.text: A goal under SDG Target 15.3 to restore degraded land and soil so that, by 2030, the world is land degradation-neutral.

facts.text: It is measured by the proportion of land that is degraded over total land area.
Desertification affects as much as one-sixth of the world's population, 70% of all drylands and one-quarter of the world's land area.

related: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

title: Illegal wildlife trade targets
article: Sustainable Development Goal 15#Target 15.c: Combat global poaching and trafficking

definition.text: SDG targets 15.7 and 15.c to end poaching and trafficking of protected species and tackle both demand and supply of illegal wildlife products.

facts.text: Illegal wildlife trade has become one of the world's largest black markets, valued at tens of billions of dollars.
Trade policies that reward sustainable use typically help wildlife populations faster than outright trade bans.
Trafficking is usually driven by organised crime and eased by corruption and weak governance.
